passage.title: Enzyme saturation

explanation: v = Vmax × 6/(2 + 6), which is three quarters of 24, or 18 µmol/min.

passage.title: Active-site turnover

question_text: What is the turnover number per active site?
explanation: Divide product formed each second by active sites: 10/2 = 5 turnovers per second.

passage.title: Activity through purification
passage.content: Before purification a sample contains 40 activity units per mg. A purified fraction contains 360 total units and 3 mg of protein.

question_text: How much has specific activity increased?

passage.title: Net glycolytic yield
passage.content: An anaerobic cell converts 6 µmol of glucose completely to lactate. Assume glucose enters as free glucose and no other pathway contributes ATP.

question_text: How much net ATP is produced?
explanation: Glycolysis spends two ATP and generates four per glucose. Lactate formation regenerates NAD+ without making extra ATP. The net yield is 2 × 6 = 12 µmol.

passage.title: Recombinant offspring
passage.content: In a testcross, 4 offspring of one recombinant type and 6 of the reciprocal type appear among 500 total. All remaining offspring have parental haplotypes.

question_text: What is the observed recombination frequency?
explanation: Count both recombinant classes. (4 + 6) / 500 × 100 = 2%.

passage.title: Recessive-allele frequency
passage.content: A large population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. A fully penetrant recessive phenotype occurs in 4 of every 10,000 individuals.

question_text: What percentage of all alleles at this locus are the recessive allele?

passage.title: Renal clearance

passage.title: Cardiac output

passage.title: Bacterial division

question_text: How many viable cells should the culture now contain?

passage.title: Protein coding length

passage.title: Buffer ratios

passage.title: The last train
passage.content: A railway manager calls the nearly empty last train wasteful. She counts the riders on that train, while a shopkeeper counts the evenings she stays in town because she knows she can leave late if she must. This does not settle whether to keep the train. It changes what a fair inquiry would measure.

question_text: Which result distinguishes recovery from reacquisition?
choice_a: The response generalizes to a bell.
choice_b: A new tone is immediately paired with food.
choice_c: The response returns without a new tone–food pairing.
explanation: Reacquisition involves renewed pairing. A return after a rest interval without reinforcement is spontaneous recovery.

passage.title: Latent learning
passage.content: Rats explore a maze without food. When food is first offered, their routes improve faster than those of rats entirely new to the maze.

question_text: Which interpretation fits the comparison?
choice_a: Food was necessary for any learning during exploration.
choice_c: Prior exploration produced learning that reward later revealed.
choice_d: The rats learned solely by watching others.
explanation: Prior experience improved later performance despite the absence of a reward during exploration.

passage.title: Proactive interference
passage.content: A volunteer learns a second locker combination but keeps entering the first one.

question_text: Which change would most directly reduce proactive interference in a new experiment?
choice_a: Shorten the delay after the first combination only.
choice_b: Ask participants to rehearse the first combination repeatedly.
choice_c: Make both combinations identical except for one digit.
choice_d: Use participants who have not learned an earlier combination.
explanation: Earlier material disrupts retrieval of newer material. Removing prior competing learning targets this mechanism.

passage.title: Source monitoring
passage.content: After a staged event, viewers read a misleading report. Several later recall a detail from the report as something they saw.

question_text: Which memory process is most directly implicated?
explanation: They retain the detail but attribute it to perception instead of the later report.

passage.title: Sensory adaptation
passage.content: A student stops noticing a constant odor but notices a different odor immediately. The original odor concentration remains stable.

question_text: Which account best fits these observations?
choice_a: A visual illusion suppressed odor intensity.
choice_b: Responsiveness to sustained stimulation has declined.
choice_c: The original odor has physically dispersed.
choice_d: The student lost all olfactory receptors.
explanation: A constant physical stimulus evokes less response while sensitivity to change remains.

passage.title: Pluralistic ignorance
passage.content: Several commuters privately suspect an emergency but each interprets the others’ calm expressions as evidence that nothing is wrong.

question_text: Which intervention targets this particular mechanism?
choice_a: Hide the distressed person from view.
choice_b: Increase the number of silent witnesses.
choice_c: Make the group larger without providing information.
choice_d: Have one witness state clearly that the situation looks dangerous.
explanation: Explicit interpretation corrects the false impression that everyone believes the situation is harmless.

passage.title: Normative influence
passage.content: A student publicly endorses the majority answer but privately gives the correct answer and says she feared ridicule.

question_text: What prediction follows most directly?
choice_b: Anonymous responding should reduce agreement with the group.
choice_c: The student will forget her private answer.
choice_d: A harder task must reduce conformity.
explanation: Anonymity reduces social costs of dissent, the motive indicated by the public–private discrepancy.

passage.title: Intergenerational mobility
passage.content: A city tracks the occupational class of adults and compares it with their parents’ class at the same age.

question_text: What additional information measures intragenerational mobility instead?
choice_c: Each adult’s own class at two points in their career
choice_d: Their neighbors’ class at the same age
explanation: Intragenerational change occurs within one person’s lifetime, unlike comparison across generations.

passage.title: Institutional discrimination
passage.content: A clinic assigns appointments only through an English telephone menu. Wait times are identical once patients get appointments, but fewer patients with limited English book visits.

question_text: Which analysis best locates the disparity?
choice_b: Compare booking completion rates by language at each menu step.
choice_c: Compare only wait times among successful callers.
explanation: Restricting analysis to booked patients removes people most affected by the access barrier.

passage.title: Construct validity
passage.content: Two observers agree perfectly when counting smiles. A team claims the count measures life satisfaction.

question_text: What evidence would most strengthen that claim?
choice_a: The count is unchanged when the same recording is replayed.
choice_b: Smile counts track independent validated measures of satisfaction in the target population.
choice_c: The observers finish at the same time.
explanation: Agreement establishes consistency. An independent measure of the intended construct addresses validity.

passage.title: Confounding
passage.content: Students who elect a tutoring program score higher than nonparticipants. Baseline motivation predicts both enrollment and scores.

question_text: Why can the difference exaggerate the effect of tutoring?
choice_a: Any large sample removes selection bias.
choice_b: Preexisting motivation may partly account for the outcome difference.
explanation: A variable related to both selection and outcome can confound the comparison.

passage.title: Cognitive appraisal
passage.content: Two participants experience similar arousal after exercise. One labels it excitement at a concert, the other anxiety before a test.

question_text: Which theory most directly emphasizes this combination?
choice_b: A pure drive-reduction account of thirst
choice_c: An account in which context has no role
explanation: The two-factor account combines physiological arousal with cognitive interpretation of context.

passage.title: Selection in clinical samples
passage.content: A researcher estimates community symptom frequency by recruiting only people already receiving specialist care.

question_text: Which concern follows most directly?
choice_a: Specialist care makes all diagnoses inaccurate.
choice_d: Care access and referral patterns affect who enters the sample.
explanation: A clinical sample can differ systematically from the population of interest even if measured accurately.

passage.title: Disulfide bonds
passage.content: A purified secreted protein runs as one band under nonreducing denaturing conditions and two smaller bands after reduction.

question_text: Which interaction most likely held its subunits together?
choice_c: A peptide bond between all subunits
explanation: Reduction cleaves disulfide links. Separating into smaller polypeptides indicates a link between chains.

passage.title: Catalysis at equilibrium
passage.content: An enzyme accelerates a reversible reaction in a closed tube. The initial substrate and product concentrations already equal their equilibrium values.

question_text: What changes immediately after enzyme addition?
choice_b: The standard free energy becomes more negative.
choice_d: Both opposing rates increase with no sustained net conversion.
explanation: Catalysis lowers the kinetic barrier in both directions without changing equilibrium.

passage.title: Respiratory uncoupling
passage.content: Isolated mitochondria receive abundant fuel and oxygen. A proton carrier makes the inner membrane permeable to protons.

question_text: Which combination is expected relative to tightly coupled respiration?
choice_a: Reduced ATP yield per oxygen consumed and a smaller proton gradient
choice_d: Increased ATP yield and a larger gradient
explanation: Leaked protons dissipate the gradient without passing through ATP synthase, reducing coupling efficiency.

passage.title: Reading frames
passage.content: A coding sequence acquires an insertion of three nucleotides between two complete codons. No stop codon is introduced.

question_text: What is the most direct consequence?
choice_a: The protein always gains three amino acids.
choice_b: One residue is added while the downstream reading frame is preserved.
choice_d: Every downstream codon shifts by one base.
explanation: Three nucleotides make one codon, so an insertion at a codon boundary leaves later grouping intact.

passage.title: Complementation
passage.content: Two recessive mutations cause the same loss of pigment. Crossing homozygous mutants yields offspring with normal pigment, assuming ordinary complementation.

question_text: Which explanation fits?
choice_a: Both parents lack the entire same pathway irreversibly.
choice_c: The mutations affect different genes and the offspring have a functional copy of each.
explanation: Each parent can supply the functional allele missing in the other mutant.

passage.title: Receptor signaling
passage.content: A mutation locks the alpha subunit of a stimulatory G protein in its GTP-bound state. The receptor ligand is washed away.

question_text: Which prediction best follows?
choice_a: The receptor must enter the nucleus.
choice_b: Downstream signaling can persist after ligand removal.
choice_d: The G protein cannot interact with effectors.
explanation: GTP hydrolysis normally terminates signaling by the alpha subunit. Locking the active state delays termination.

passage.title: Endocrine feedback
passage.content: An experimental infusion raises circulating thyroid hormone in an animal with an intact hypothalamic–pituitary axis.

question_text: Which early compensatory response is expected?
choice_c: Increased stimulation of thyroid hormone synthesis by TSH
explanation: Negative feedback from thyroid hormone reduces stimulation of the thyroid by the upstream axis.

passage.title: Antigen presentation
passage.content: A virus infects a nucleated cell. Peptides from viral proteins synthesized in its cytosol are presented at the cell surface.

question_text: Which pairing most directly supports recognition of the infected cell?
choice_a: MHC I with a CD8 T cell
choice_c: Free antibody with a T-cell receptor as its antigen
explanation: Cytosolic peptides commonly enter the MHC I pathway and are surveyed by CD8 T cells.

passage.title: Horizontal gene transfer
passage.content: Bacteria acquire a marker from a cell-free filtrate containing disrupted donor cells. DNase treatment abolishes transfer.

question_text: Which mechanism best fits the result?
explanation: Sensitivity to DNase and transfer without donor contact support uptake of exposed DNA.

passage.title: Competitive substitution mechanisms
passage.content: Two substrates react with the same nucleophile. Increasing nucleophile concentration doubles the initial rate for substrate A but leaves the rate for B unchanged.

question_text: Which simple mechanism is consistent with the data for A?
choice_b: A zero-order process in both reactants
choice_d: Unimolecular ionization as the sole slow step
explanation: Dependence on nucleophile concentration supports its involvement in the rate-determining event; by itself it does not establish every mechanistic detail.

passage.title: Isotope peaks
passage.content: A molecular-ion cluster displays M and M+2 peaks of nearly equal intensity. The unknown contains one halogen atom.

question_text: Which atom best explains this pattern?
explanation: Naturally abundant bromine has two principal isotopes in near-equal proportions. A single chlorine instead gives roughly a three-to-one pattern.

passage.title: Carbonyl spectroscopy
passage.content: A neutral compound shows a strong carbonyl absorption and a very broad O–H band extending well below 3000 cm⁻¹.

question_text: Which functional group best fits both observations?
explanation: A carboxylic acid contains a carbonyl and a characteristically broad hydrogen-bonded O–H stretch.

passage.title: Acyl substitution
passage.content: An amine reacts with an acyl chloride under conditions that remove the acid produced.

question_text: Which group leaves the tetrahedral intermediate as the carbonyl reforms?
explanation: Addition of the nucleophile is followed by collapse of the intermediate and loss of chloride.

passage.title: Stereospecific inversion
passage.content: An enantiopure secondary substrate undergoes a single concerted backside displacement at the stereocenter.

question_text: Which outcome follows even if substituent priority changes?
choice_b: Inversion of geometry at the reacting carbon
choice_c: Retention of geometry at every atom
choice_d: The R label must become S
explanation: Backside attack inverts the spatial arrangement. The R/S label also depends on the priority order in the product.

passage.title: Free energy and coupling
passage.content: Reaction A has positive standard free energy. The cell couples it chemically to a strongly favorable reaction B.

question_text: When is the coupled standard process favorable?
choice_a: Whenever A has a large activation barrier
choice_b: Whenever B occurs in a different compartment without coupling
choice_c: When the sum of the two standard free energies is negative
choice_d: Only when both reactions have positive standard free energy
explanation: Free energies add for appropriately combined reactions. The combined sign determines standard thermodynamic favorability.

passage.title: Reaction quotient
passage.content: For a reversible reaction the measured reaction quotient is smaller than the equilibrium constant at the same temperature.

question_text: What net change will move the mixture toward equilibrium?
choice_b: An increase in the equilibrium constant
explanation: Forward reaction increases the product-to-reactant ratio toward the equilibrium value.

passage.title: Buffer capacity
passage.content: Two buffers have equal acid-to-base ratios. Buffer X contains ten times the total buffer concentration of Y, at equal volumes.

question_text: What happens when the same small amount of strong acid is added to each?
choice_a: The buffer ratio cannot change in either vessel.
choice_b: X generally undergoes a smaller pH change.
choice_c: X must start one pH unit higher.
explanation: X has more conjugate base available to neutralize the acid, so its ratio shifts less.

passage.title: Salt bridge function
passage.content: A galvanic cell initially delivers current. The salt bridge is removed while the wire remains connected.

question_text: Why does the current rapidly decline?
choice_a: Electrons normally travel through the salt bridge.
choice_b: The equilibrium constant instantly becomes zero.
choice_c: The cathode becomes a source of protons in every cell.
choice_d: Charge separation opposes continued electron transfer.
explanation: Ion migration normally maintains bulk electroneutrality in each half-cell.

passage.title: Momentum and sticking
passage.content: Two carts collide on a horizontal frictionless track and stick together.

question_text: Which quantity must be conserved for the two-cart system during the collision?
explanation: With negligible external impulse, system momentum is conserved even though kinetic energy can become internal energy.

passage.title: Refraction
passage.content: Light enters a transparent medium of higher refractive index from air at oblique incidence.

question_text: What happens to its frequency and wavelength?
choice_a: Frequency stays constant and wavelength shortens.
choice_d: Frequency falls and wavelength stays fixed.
explanation: The source fixes frequency at the boundary. Light travels more slowly in the higher-index medium, so its wavelength decreases.

passage.title: Induction through a loop
passage.content: A rigid conducting loop rotates in a uniform static magnetic field. Its area stays fixed.

question_text: Which change permits an induced electromotive force?
choice_a: A decrease in its circumference alone with fixed flux
choice_b: A change in magnetic flux through the loop
choice_c: A steady flux of any magnitude
choice_d: An increase in the loop’s mass
explanation: Rotation can change the projected area perpendicular to the field. Faraday’s law depends on the rate of change of flux.

passage.title: Actor and observer
passage.content: A student blames a stranger’s missed deadline on laziness but describes her own missed deadline as a consequence of an outage.

question_text: Which asymmetry is illustrated?
explanation: The same behavior is attributed to a disposition for another person and a situation for oneself.

passage.title: Reducing prejudice
passage.content: Two competing groups must coordinate different skills to repair the only shared water line. Neither can finish alone.

question_text: Which mechanism best fits the intervention?
choice_a: Independent competition for the same prize
explanation: A valued goal requiring both groups creates positive interdependence.

passage.title: Context-dependent retrieval
passage.content: Divers learn word lists underwater or on land and are tested in either setting. Performance improves when learning and test settings match.

question_text: What is the strongest interpretation?
choice_c: Matched settings enlarge sensory memory capacity.
explanation: The benefit depends on matching contexts rather than either setting alone.

passage.title: Perceptual set
passage.content: The same ambiguous mark is usually read as B between A and C and as 13 between 12 and 14.

question_text: What does this show?
choice_b: The retina detects two different physical marks.
choice_c: All recognition is independent of prior knowledge.
explanation: Identical visual input is interpreted differently because the surrounding sequence creates expectations.

passage.title: Fixed-interval schedules
passage.content: A pigeon receives food for the first peck after each two-minute interval. Earlier pecks do not reset the clock.

question_text: Which behavior pattern is most plausible after training?
choice_a: A pause followed by increasing responding near the interval’s end
choice_b: Perfectly constant responding independent of elapsed time by definition
choice_c: A reward determined only by total pecks
explanation: On a fixed-interval schedule the passage of time changes when a response can next produce reinforcement.

passage.title: Observer expectancy
passage.content: An investigator knows who received a training intervention and rates ambiguous performances more favorably for those participants.

question_text: Which change best targets this bias?
choice_a: Increase the length of the rating form only.
choice_b: Mask the rater to group assignment.
choice_d: Recruit only participants who expect improvement.
explanation: Masking removes knowledge of condition that could influence scoring.

passage.title: Incidence versus prevalence
passage.content: A disorder’s onset rate is stable while people live longer after diagnosis, with no change in case detection or remission.

question_text: What trend would be expected in a stable population?
choice_c: Every new case is counted twice as incident.
choice_d: Prevalence may rise despite stable incidence.
explanation: Longer duration increases the number living with the condition at a given time.

passage.title: Secondary immune responses
passage.content: A previously exposed host produces high-affinity antibody rapidly after re-exposure to the same antigen.

question_text: Which cell population best accounts for the speed and specificity?
explanation: Expanded memory populations can respond more rapidly to the antigen encountered previously.

passage.title: Oxygen affinity
passage.content: At the same oxygen partial pressure a hemoglobin sample has lower saturation after an increase in hydrogen ion concentration.

question_text: What physiological effect is consistent with that change?
choice_a: Tighter oxygen binding at every tissue pressure
choice_b: Enhanced oxygen unloading in acidic tissue
choice_c: Loss of all cooperative binding necessarily
choice_d: Conversion of oxygen directly to carbon dioxide
explanation: Increased acidity can stabilize lower-affinity hemoglobin states and facilitate unloading.

passage.title: Regenerating NAD+
passage.content: A fermentation-deficient cell has abundant glucose but limited oxygen. Its cytosolic NADH rises and NAD+ falls.

question_text: Why can glycolysis slow?
choice_a: Glycolysis directly uses molecular oxygen in every step.
choice_b: NADH is the substrate of hexokinase.
choice_c: A glycolytic oxidation step requires NAD+ as an electron acceptor.
explanation: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase requires NAD+. Fermentation can regenerate it when respiration is limited.

passage.title: Cell-cycle controls
passage.content: A checkpoint normally prevents entry into mitosis while DNA replication is incomplete. An inhibitor disables that checkpoint.

question_text: Which observation most directly supports loss of checkpoint function?
choice_a: Cells enter mitosis with incompletely replicated chromosomes.
choice_c: Cells stop before S phase in every case.
explanation: The observation links premature mitotic entry to the condition that should block it.

passage.title: Splicing and expression
passage.content: Two tissues express transcripts from one gene with different combinations of internal exons. Their genomic sequences match.

question_text: Which mechanism best explains the difference?
choice_b: A change in every promoter sequence
choice_c: Different genetic codes in the two tissues
choice_d: Independent deletion of identical DNA in both tissues
explanation: Differential inclusion of exons during RNA processing can produce distinct mature transcripts from one gene.

passage.title: Filtration and reabsorption
passage.content: A solute is freely filtered, neither secreted nor made by the kidney, and is present in urine at an excretion rate below its filtered load.

question_text: What follows from mass balance?
choice_d: The filtration rate must be zero.
explanation: Excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion. A positive shortfall with no secretion implies reabsorption.

passage.title: Detecting selection
passage.content: Two bacterial lineages are mixed at equal frequencies. In replicate drug-treated cultures one lineage consistently increases; in untreated controls their frequencies fluctuate around the initial values.

question_text: Which inference is most defensible?
choice_a: The drug directed every mutation toward resistance.
choice_b: The favored lineage has higher relative fitness under the tested drug condition.
choice_c: The lineage necessarily grows faster in every environment.
choice_d: Random genetic drift must always favor that lineage.
explanation: A reproducible condition-dependent frequency change supports selection under treatment while leaving its mechanism open.

passage.title: The empty square
passage.content: City planners photographed a public square at noon and found no one there. A night vendor asked why they had chosen noon. A second team sampled the square at six different hours and found a crowd just after the factories closed. The first photograph was honest. What it could not do was appoint itself representative of an entire day. The second survey, too, could mislead if all six visits fell on a holiday.

question_text: What does the writer criticize?
choice_c: The use of photographs in all inquiries.
choice_d: Treating a limited observation as representative without justification.
explanation: The writer accepts the photograph’s accuracy while questioning the scope of the inference.

passage.title: The empty square

question_text: Why does the holiday matter?
choice_a: Several observations can share the same sampling bias.
choice_b: It guarantees that both findings are false.
choice_c: It makes the first survey more detailed.
choice_d: It shows that crowds never gather after work.
explanation: More observations do not solve a selection problem if all are drawn from an atypical day.

explanation: Variation in both time of day and type of day matters to the generalization being made.

passage.title: Who wrote the recipe?
passage.content: A baker’s notebook contains exact weights for flour but only a gesture sketched beside the word knead. An editor proposes replacing the gesture with ten minutes. It would make the page easier to follow, she says. The baker agrees for one kitchen on one day. In a colder room or with a different flour, the clock may be less reliable than the hand. A written recipe need not ban measurement; it may need to teach the reader which changes to measure.

question_text: Why might ten minutes be inadequate?
choice_b: It is too short in every kitchen.
choice_d: It replaces a judgment sensitive to conditions with a fixed duration.
explanation: The author names temperature and flour as conditions under which time alone can mislead.

question_text: What does the precise flour weight establish?
choice_a: The notebook was written for machines.
choice_d: Every ingredient must have the same mass.
explanation: The example blocks the interpretation that the baker rejects all precision.

passage.title: Chiral separations
passage.content: Two pure enantiomers show a single unresolved peak on an achiral chromatography column under conditions with no other chiral agents.

question_text: Which change most directly enables different retention times?
choice_a: Replace the detector with a brighter lamp.
choice_b: Use a longer achiral column with otherwise identical interactions.
explanation: A chiral phase permits diastereomeric interactions of unequal strength with the two enantiomers.
